problem: Existing outdoor navigation benchmarks are either low in photorealism and complexity (3D simulators like CARLA, MetaUrban), lack dynamics and continuous navigation (Street View based), or use short clips (Vid2Sim). None supports district-scale, ground-level egocentric exploration in realistic, dynamic streets.
motivation: Urban assistants (e.g. for getting lost or for blind users) need agents that can perceive, localize, plan and reason spatially in real city streets. A benchmark built from real 360° video gives photorealistic, dynamic street-level observations across a whole district, so agents can be tested on diverse capabilities under realistic conditions.
key_idea: Build a benchmark on a Realistic Virtual World of Akihabara (a pose graph of 602 360° video segments) with 175 human-crafted tasks in 7 subcategories, and evaluate LMM-based agents against local-expert humans.
insight: LMM agents are far below humans (best model Gemini 2.5 Flash 17.1% overall vs human 77.3%), and performance drops as difficulty rises. Giving a map-based location prior does not help consistently: GPT-5 Rel Reason fell 48.0→32.0 with location, and Landmark Lang 24.0→16.0, suggesting poor map-to-visual alignment. Failure analysis shows model-specific patterns: GPT-5 fails mostly by exploration (55%), Gemini and InternVL by low-level action errors (~40%), and perception failures surge in spatial reasoning.
method: Environment: 360° video segments (602 over 85 streets) projected onto spheres and organized as a navigable Unity pose graph (193 nodes, 305 edges, mean branching degree 3.16), covering ~750 m x 650 m around Akihabara Station.

Task suite: 3 categories and 7 subcategories with 25 tasks each (Localization, Landmark Search Language/Image, Map Navigation, VLN, Relational Spatial Reasoning, Object Count). Tasks were hand-made by annotators who had visited Akihabara, and each is labeled Easy/Medium/Hard.

Evaluation: exact_match (Localization on 5x5 grid), fuzzy_match (GPT-5 judge, 97.9% agreement with humans), coordinate_match (final position within 10 m, or 20 m for Map Nav), and MRA for Object Count.

Baseline agent: a ReAct-style LMM agent with a reflection memory and 7 discrete actions (forward, tilt up/down, rotate left/right, reset view, answer), plus branch-selection actions at intersections. Inputs are the current view, an OpenStreetMap location map with agent marker, task reference images, and memory.
Stopping conditions: 50-step limit, stagnation (same action 20 times without moving), and moving away from the goal 5 times in a row.
Analysis: ablation without location map, and failure classification (Action / Grounding / Perception / Explore / Planning) by Gemini 3 Flash with human verification.

setting.backbone: GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct, InternVL3.5-8B/38B (all frozen, prompted)
setting.training_data: none (training-free, prompted LMM agents; benchmark only)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB view from 360° video with controllable camera heading/tilt, plus an optional top-down OpenStreetMap image with location marker and orientation
setting.action_space: 7 discrete actions (forward, look up/down/left/right, reset view, answer) plus branch-direction actions at intersections; move and rotate magnitude given as SMALL/MEDIUM/LARGE
setting.simulator: Unity 6 (custom pose-graph environment built from 360° videos of Akihabara)
setting.privileged: none (the map with current location is given as input in the main setting; the w/o-location ablation removes it)

results: All LMM agents fall far below local-expert humans (77.3% average vs 17.1% for the best, Gemini 2.5 Flash). GPT-5 is best on Landmark (Img) with 48.0 and Rel Reason with 32.0, and Map Navigation is near 0% for nearly all models. Image goals are generally easier than language goals, and accuracy falls with difficulty.
limitations: Only one district (Akihabara) and navigation restricted to pre-recorded trajectories with discontinuities at boundaries and no physical interaction
Small benchmark (175 tasks, 25 per subcategory), so results are noisy, with success rates in multiples of 4%; difficulty labels are partly subjective
Results conflate spatial reasoning with controller and prompt brittleness (Action/Explore failures), and there are few models and no trained navigation agents
